title: Land of the Blind
full_review:
That fine English actor Ralph Fiennes has a way of elevating whatever project to which he lends his talents, and "Land of the Blind" (Bauer Martinez) is no exception, but the film emerges nonetheless as a disappointing and sadly misguided political satire.

Donald Sutherland plays Thorne, a jailed playwright turned terrorist, who when we first see him is a disheveled wreck, writing on the walls of his cell with his own excrement. Military man Joe (Fiennes) is assigned to guard him, and gradually comes under Thorne's sway and belief that it is necessary to take up arms against an oppressor.

Upon release from prison, Thorne -- with Joe's help -- assassinates the crazy-as-a-loon president Maximilian (Tom Hollander) before the tyrant can kill him. But then (as history has often shown to be the case) Thorne imposes an even more repressive regime of his own.

When an increasingly disenchanted Joe, now an officer, refuses to sign a loyalty oath, even knowing his wife and child might be at risk, he's arrested and thrown into prison himself for brutal reconditioning, and the authorities do what they can to erase him from history.

Writer-director Robert Edwards, an ex-Army infantry and intelligence officer making his feature film debut, attempts to leaven the grim tale with sardonically humorous moments, but they come across as utterly lame. Fiennes does indeed deliver his accustomed superlative performance, and there's lively, if over the top, work from Hollander as the mad dictator who, with his imperious first lady (Lara Flynn Boyle) comes to a bloody end.

The heavy-duty expletives -- and occasional sexual elements including some hard-core sex talk, as for instance, when the dictator frolics with his power-mad wife -- seem dramatically gratuitous, and give this film, which opened the Human Rights Watch International Film Festival, a trashy veneer.

The themes about the corrupting of power, prison abuse, and erosion of journalism into infotainment, with no doubt several contemporary parallels intended, are valid, but as presented here, are derivative and boringly predictable.

Throughout, there is much baffling elephant imagery. Turkey footage would have been more appropriate.

The film contains pervasive rough language and crude expressions, some profanity and irreligiosity, sexual situations and partial nudity, violence and brutality, and gratuitous scatological elements. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
